tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture?

A. Sand and water
B. Air
C. Sodium chloride
D. Iron filings and sulfur powder
ms: **B.** Air is a mixture of gases (mainly $\ce{N2}$, $\ce{O2}$ and $\ce{Ar}$) with uniform composition throughout, so it is a homogeneous mixture. A and D are heterogeneous mixtures (the components can be seen as separate phases); C is a compound, not a mixture.

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
A pure solid is heated and is melting at its melting point. Which statement is correct?

A. The average kinetic energy of the particles increases.
B. The energy absorbed is used to overcome some of the attractive forces between the particles.
C. The temperature of the sample rises steadily until all of the solid has melted.
D. The particles become completely separated from one another.
ms: **B.** During melting the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy of the particles does not change (A and C are wrong); the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the particles by overcoming some of the attractive forces. Particles in a liquid are still close together, so D describes boiling, not melting.

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
Which statements are correct for **all** mixtures?

I. The components keep their individual chemical properties.
II. The components are present in a fixed ratio by mass.
III. The components can be separated by physical methods.

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **B.** In a mixture the components are not chemically bonded, so they keep their own properties and can be separated by physical means (filtration, distillation, chromatography etc.). A fixed ratio by mass (II) is a property of a compound, not a mixture, so A, C and D are wrong.

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
Which sample contains particles with the greatest average kinetic energy?

A. Helium gas at $250\ \text{K}$
B. Liquid water at $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$
C. Nitrogen gas at $-10\ ^\circ\text{C}$
D. Solid iron at $30\ ^\circ\text{C}$
ms: **D.** Average kinetic energy is directly proportional to the absolute (kelvin) temperature and does not depend on the state or the mass of the particles. Temperatures in kelvin: A $250\ \text{K}$, B $298\ \text{K}$, C $263\ \text{K}$, D $303\ \text{K}$, so D is highest. Students who think gases always have more kinetic energy than solids choose A or C.

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
A student heated $100.0\ \text{g}$ of a pure solid substance, X, in an insulated container with an electric heater supplying energy at a constant rate of $50.0\ \text{W}$ ($50.0\ \text{J s}^{-1}$). The temperature was recorded every 30 seconds. The results are shown in the graph (illustrative data).

![Heating curve: temperature rises from 20 °C at A to 80 °C at B (4 min), stays at 80 °C until C (9 min), then rises to 116 °C at D (12 min)](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.1_5.svg)

(a) State the melting point of X. [1]

(b) State the physical state or states of X present between points B and C. [1]

(c) Explain, in terms of particles, why the temperature remains constant between B and C. [2]

(d) Calculate the energy, in $\text{J g}^{-1}$, absorbed by X to melt it completely. Assume that all the energy from the heater is absorbed by X. [2]

(e) Suggest, with a reason, how heat loss to the surroundings would affect your answer to (d) compared with the true value. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $80\ ^\circ\text{C}$ ✓ (Accept $353\ \text{K}$.)

(b)
- solid **and** liquid ✓

(c)
- energy absorbed is used to overcome (some of the) attractive forces between particles / increases the potential energy of particles ✓
- average kinetic energy of the particles does not change (so temperature stays constant) ✓

(d)
- time of melting $= 9 - 4 = 5\ \text{min} = 300\ \text{s}$; energy $= 50.0 \times 300 = 1.50 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J}$ ✓
- $\dfrac{1.50 \times 10^{4}}{100.0} = 150\ \text{J g}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Award [1 max] for $1.50 \times 10^{4}$ (not divided by mass) or for using the time in minutes instead of seconds ($50.0 \times 5 \div 100.0 = 2.5\ \text{J g}^{-1}$) if otherwise correct.

(e)
- calculated value too high/greater than true value **because** some of the energy supplied is lost to the surroundings rather than absorbed by X ✓

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
(a) Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas. [3]

(b) Solid iodine changes directly into a gas when warmed gently.

(i) State the term for this change of state. [1]

(ii) State the term for the reverse change, from gas directly to solid. [1]

(c) Explain, using the kinetic molecular theory, why a gas can be compressed much more easily than a liquid. [1]
ms:
(a)
- solid: particles closely packed in a regular arrangement **and** vibrate about fixed positions ✓
- liquid: particles close together but randomly arranged **and** move/slide past one another ✓
- gas: particles far apart (randomly arranged) **and** move rapidly in straight lines/randomly in all directions ✓

Award [1 max] if arrangement is correct for all three but movement is not described (or vice versa).

(b)(i)
- sublimation ✓

(b)(ii)
- deposition ✓

(c)
- (large) spaces between gas particles so particles can be pushed closer together, whereas liquid particles are already touching/close together ✓

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
(a) A student is given a mixture of sand and sodium chloride. Outline how the student could obtain a pure, dry sample of sodium chloride crystals from the mixture. [4]

(b) A food colouring, M, was analysed by paper chromatography alongside two reference dyes, R1 and R2. The chromatogram is shown.

![Paper chromatogram: solvent front 8.0 cm above the baseline; M shows spots at 3.2 cm and 6.0 cm, R1 one spot at 6.0 cm, R2 one spot at 4.5 cm](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.1_7.svg)

(i) Calculate the $R_\text{F}$ value of the lower spot in M. [1]

(ii) Deduce which reference dye is present in M. [1]

(c) Explain why the components of M travel different distances up the paper. [2]
ms:
(a)
- add (warm) water to dissolve the sodium chloride / stir ✓
- filter to remove the sand (sand stays as residue) ✓
- evaporate the filtrate until crystals start to form / heat to reduce volume, then leave to cool and crystallize ✓
- collect crystals by filtration **and** dry them (e.g. between filter papers / in a low oven / desiccator) ✓

Accept evaporating the filtrate to dryness for M3 but M4 still requires a drying step or a valid statement that the solid is dry.

(b)(i)
- $R_\text{F} = \dfrac{3.2}{8.0} = 0.40$ ✓

(b)(ii)
- R1 **and** its spot travels the same distance/has the same $R_\text{F}$ ($0.75$) as one spot in M ✓

(c)
- components have different (relative) solubilities in the solvent/mobile phase ✓
- **and** different attractions to/affinity for the paper/stationary phase (water in the paper) ✓

Accept "different partition between mobile and stationary phases" for [2].

tname: Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
text:
Samples of helium gas and argon gas are both at $300\ \text{K}$.

(a) State the relationship between the kelvin temperature of a substance and the average kinetic energy of its particles. [1]

(b) Compare the average kinetic energy and the average speed of the particles in the two samples. Explain your answer. [3]

(c) Calculate the temperature, in $^\circ\text{C}$, at which the average kinetic energy of the helium atoms would be twice its value at $25.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$. [2]

(d) A student states that heating a gas from $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $40\ ^\circ\text{C}$ doubles the average kinetic energy of its particles. Evaluate this statement. [2]
ms:
(a)
- average kinetic energy is (directly) proportional to the absolute/kelvin temperature ✓

(b)
- average kinetic energy is the same (same temperature) ✓
- helium atoms move faster/have greater average speed ✓
- helium atoms have smaller mass, so for the same $E_\text{k} = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ they must have a greater speed ✓

(c)
- $T = 2 \times 298.15 = 596.3\ \text{K}$ ✓ (Accept $2 \times 298 = 596\ \text{K}$.)
- $596.3 - 273.15 = 323\ ^\circ\text{C}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Do **not** award M2 for $50\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

(d)
- statement is incorrect: kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, not Celsius temperature ✓
- $T$ increases from $293\ \text{K}$ to $313\ \text{K}$, so kinetic energy increases by a factor of only about $1.07$ / by about $7\ \%$ ✓

text:
Which species contains 18 electrons and 20 neutrons?

A. $\ce{^{35}Cl-}$
B. $\ce{^{37}Cl}$
C. $\ce{^{37}Cl-}$
D. $\ce{^{40}Ar}$
ms: **C.** $\ce{^{37}Cl-}$ has $17$ protons, $37 - 17 = 20$ neutrons and $17 + 1 = 18$ electrons. A has 18 electrons but only 18 neutrons; B has 20 neutrons but only 17 electrons; D has 18 electrons but 22 neutrons.

text:
Which statement about the subatomic particles in an atom is correct?

A. Protons and neutrons have the same relative charge.
B. The mass of an electron is about $\tfrac{1}{2000}$ of the mass of a proton.
C. Most of the volume of an atom is occupied by the nucleus.
D. Protons and electrons are both found in the nucleus.
ms: **B.** The relative mass of an electron is $5 \times 10^{-4}$ (about $1/1836$) of that of a proton. Protons have charge $+1$ and neutrons $0$ (A); the nucleus is tiny compared with the atom, which is mostly empty space (C); electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus (D).

text:
Hydrogen gas can be made from the isotope $\ce{^{1}H}$ only or from the isotope $\ce{^{2}H}$ only. Which properties differ between $\ce{^{1}H2}$ and $\ce{^{2}H2}$ gases at the same temperature and pressure?

I. Density
II. Average speed of the molecules
III. Electron configuration of the atoms

A. I only
B. I and II only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **B.** The isotopes differ in mass (number of neutrons), so physical properties that depend on mass differ: $\ce{^{2}H2}$ is denser and, at the same temperature (same average kinetic energy), its molecules move more slowly. Both isotopes have one electron, $1\text{s}^1$, so III is the same and chemical properties are essentially the same.

text:
The mass spectrum of a sample of gallium is shown.

![Mass spectrum of gallium: peaks at m/z 69 (60.1 %) and m/z 71 (39.9 %)](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.2_4.svg)

What is the relative atomic mass of gallium in this sample?

A. $69.8$
B. $70.0$
C. $70.2$
D. $71.0$
ms: **A.** $A_\text{r} = \dfrac{(69 \times 60.1) + (71 \times 39.9)}{100} = 41.47 + 28.33 = 69.8$. B is the unweighted mean of the two masses; C comes from swapping the abundances; D ignores the more abundant isotope. The weighted mean must lie closer to $69$ because $\ce{^{69}Ga}$ is more abundant.

text:
Chlorine consists of the isotopes $\ce{^{35}Cl}$ ($75\ \%$) and $\ce{^{37}Cl}$ ($25\ \%$). In the mass spectrum of chlorine gas, peaks for the molecular ions $\ce{Cl2+}$ appear at $m/z = 70$, $72$ and $74$.

What is the ratio of the heights of these three peaks?

A. $3 : 1 : 0$
B. $9 : 6 : 1$
C. $3 : 2 : 1$
D. $9 : 3 : 1$
ms: **B.** Probabilities: $\ce{^{35}Cl^{35}Cl}$ $= 0.75^2 = 0.5625$; $\ce{^{35}Cl^{37}Cl}$ (two ways) $= 2 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.375$; $\ce{^{37}Cl^{37}Cl}$ $= 0.25^2 = 0.0625$, giving $9 : 6 : 1$. D forgets that the mixed molecule can form in two ways; A and C do not multiply the probabilities.

text:
The mass spectrum of a sample of magnesium is shown. Assume that the relative mass of each isotope is equal to its mass number.

![Mass spectrum of magnesium: m/z 24 (78.99 %), m/z 25 (10.00 %), m/z 26 (11.01 %)](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.2_6.svg)

(a) Calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium in this sample, to two decimal places. [2]

(b) State the number of neutrons in an atom of the heaviest isotope. [1]

(c) A very small additional peak is observed at $m/z = 12$. Suggest the identity of the species responsible for this peak. [1]

(d) Explain why the three isotopes of magnesium have the same chemical properties. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $(24 \times 78.99) + (25 \times 10.00) + (26 \times 11.01)$ divided by $100$ ✓
- $A_\text{r} = 24.32$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Award [1 max] for $24.3$ (not to two decimal places) only if working is shown and correct.

(b)
- $14$ ✓

(c)
- $\ce{^{24}Mg^{2+}}$ / a doubly charged ion of magnesium-24 ($m = 24$, $z = 2$) ✓

Do not accept $\ce{^{12}C+}$ (the sample is magnesium) unless contamination is explicitly argued; do not accept $\ce{Mg+}$.

(d)
- same number of protons and electrons / same electron configuration (chemical properties depend on electrons, not neutrons) ✓

text:
(a) Complete the table. [3]

| Species | Number of protons | Number of neutrons | Number of electrons |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\ce{^{27}Al^{3+}}$ | | | |
| $\ce{^{32}S^{2-}}$ | | | |
| | $20$ | $20$ | $18$ |

(b) Define the term *isotopes*. [1]

(c) Explain why the relative atomic mass of chlorine, $35.45$, is not a whole number. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $\ce{^{27}Al^{3+}}$: $13$, $14$, $10$ ✓
- $\ce{^{32}S^{2-}}$: $16$, $16$, $18$ ✓
- $\ce{^{40}Ca^{2+}}$ ✓ (both mass number and charge required)

(b)
- atoms of the same element / with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons ✓

Do not accept "same atomic number, different mass" without reference to neutrons **or** mass number.

(c)
- chlorine consists of a mixture of isotopes ($\ce{^{35}Cl}$ and $\ce{^{37}Cl}$) and $A_\text{r}$ is the weighted mean of their masses ✓

text:
In the gold foil experiment, a beam of positively charged alpha particles was directed at a very thin sheet of gold.

(a) Describe **two** observations made in this experiment and state what each one showed about the structure of the atom. [4]

(b) The radius of a typical atom is about $1 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}$ and the radius of its nucleus is about $1 \times 10^{-15}\ \text{m}$. Calculate how many times greater the volume of the atom is than the volume of its nucleus. Assume both are spheres. [2]

(c) Explain why almost all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus. [1]
ms:
(a)
- most alpha particles passed straight through (undeflected) ✓
- so the atom is mostly empty space ✓
- a few alpha particles were deflected through large angles/bounced back ✓
- so the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus ✓

Award [1] for each observation and [1] for each correct deduction linked to it.

(b)
- volume $\propto r^3$, so ratio $= \left(\dfrac{1 \times 10^{-10}}{1 \times 10^{-15}}\right)^3$ ✓
- $1 \times 10^{15}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for $1 \times 10^{5}$ (ratio of radii).

(c)
- protons and neutrons (in the nucleus) each have relative mass of about $1$, whereas electrons have negligible mass ($5 \times 10^{-4}$) ✓

text:
Boron has two naturally occurring isotopes, $\ce{^{10}B}$ and $\ce{^{11}B}$. The relative atomic mass of naturally occurring boron is $10.81$. Assume the relative mass of each isotope equals its mass number.

(a) Calculate the percentage abundance of each isotope in naturally occurring boron. [2]

(b) Sketch the mass spectrum you would expect for naturally occurring boron. Label the axes. [2]

(c) Boron used to absorb neutrons in nuclear reactors is enriched in $\ce{^{10}B}$. A sample of enriched boron has a relative atomic mass of $10.40$. Calculate the percentage of $\ce{^{10}B}$ in this sample. [1]

(d) State **one** property that differs between a sample of enriched boron and naturally occurring boron. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $10x + 11(1 - x) = 10.81$ / $10x + 11(100 - x) = 1081$ ✓
- $\ce{^{10}B} = 19\ \%$ **and** $\ce{^{11}B} = 81\ \%$ ✓

(b)
- axes labelled $m/z$ **and** relative abundance (or percentage abundance) ✓
- two lines at $m/z = 10$ and $11$ with the line at $11$ about four times taller than the line at $10$ (consistent with (a)) ✓

![Expected mass spectrum of boron: lines at m/z 10 (19 %) and 11 (81 %)](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.2_9-2.svg)

(c)
- $60\ \%$ ✓ ($10y + 11(1 - y) = 10.40$, $y = 0.60$)

(d)
- density / mass of a given volume / rate of diffusion (of a boron compound) / nuclear property such as ability to absorb neutrons ✓

Do not accept chemical properties or reactivity.

text:
Deuterium, $\ce{^{2}H}$ (symbol D), is an isotope of hydrogen. Heavy water, $\ce{D2O}$, contains deuterium in place of $\ce{^{1}H}$.

(a) State the composition of the nucleus of a deuterium atom. [1]

(b) Determine the total number of neutrons in one molecule of $\ce{D2^{16}O}$. [1]

(c) Calculate the relative molecular mass of $\ce{D2O}$. Use $A_\text{r}(\text{D}) = 2.01$ and $A_\text{r}(\text{O}) = 16.00$. [1]

(d) The boiling point of $\ce{D2O}$ is $101.4\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and that of $\ce{H2O}$ is $100.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$, yet both react in the same way with sodium. Explain these observations. [2]

(e) Water molecules can be made from any combination of the isotopes $\ce{^{1}H}$, $\ce{^{2}H}$, $\ce{^{16}O}$ and $\ce{^{18}O}$. Deduce the number of different relative molecular masses that are possible, assuming the relative mass of each isotope equals its mass number. [2]
ms:
(a)
- one proton **and** one neutron ✓

(b)
- $10$ ✓ ($2 \times 1$ from D, $8$ from $\ce{^{16}O}$)

(c)
- $20.02$ ✓

(d)
- physical properties (such as boiling point) depend on the mass of the molecules/particles, and $\ce{D2O}$ molecules are heavier ✓
- chemical properties depend on electrons/electron configuration, which are the same for both isotopes of hydrogen ✓

(e)
- hydrogen pairs give masses $2$, $3$ or $4$ **and** oxygen gives $16$ or $18$ / lists possible values $18, 19, 20, 20, 21, 22$ ✓
- $5$ different values ($18, 19, 20, 21, 22$) ✓

Award [1 max] for $6$ (not recognizing that $\ce{^{1}H2^{18}O}$ and $\ce{^{2}H2^{16}O}$ both have mass $20$).

text:
What is the electron configuration of a sulfur atom in its ground state?

A. $[\text{Ne}]\,3\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{p}^{4}$
B. $[\text{Ne}]\,3\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{p}^{6}$
C. $[\text{Ne}]\,3\text{s}^{1}\,3\text{p}^{5}$
D. $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{p}^{4}$
ms: **A.** Sulfur has $16$ electrons: $10$ in the neon core then $3\text{s}^2\,3\text{p}^4$. B is the sulfide ion $\ce{S^2-}$; C is an excited state (or ignores filling order); D uses the wrong noble-gas core (argon already has $18$ electrons).

text:
What is the electron configuration of the $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ion?

A. $[\text{Ar}]\,4\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{d}^{4}$
B. $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{6}$
C. $[\text{Ar}]\,4\text{s}^{1}\,3\text{d}^{5}$
D. $[\text{Ar}]\,4\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{d}^{6}$
ms: **B.** Fe is $[\text{Ar}]\,4\text{s}^2\,3\text{d}^6$ (D); when transition elements form ions, the 4s electrons are removed first, giving $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^6$. A removes the electrons from 3d instead of 4s; C is incorrectly modelled on the Cr exception.

text:
Which electron transition in a hydrogen atom emits a photon with the **shortest** wavelength?

A. $n = 2 \rightarrow n = 1$
B. $n = 3 \rightarrow n = 2$
C. $n = 4 \rightarrow n = 2$
D. $n = 1 \rightarrow n = 3$
ms: **A.** Shortest wavelength means highest photon energy. Energy levels converge at higher $n$, so the gap between $n = 2$ and $n = 1$ is much larger than any transition ending at $n = 2$ (B, C, which are visible lines). D is an absorption (electron moves to a higher level), so no photon is emitted.

text:
Which statement explains why the first ionization energy of sulfur is lower than that of phosphorus?

A. Sulfur has a greater nuclear charge than phosphorus.
B. The electron removed from sulfur comes from a 3p orbital that already contains another electron, so it experiences extra repulsion.
C. The electron removed from sulfur comes from a 3s orbital.
D. The atomic radius of sulfur is larger than that of phosphorus.
ms: **B.** P is $3\text{s}^2\,3\text{p}^3$ (one electron in each 3p orbital); S is $3\text{s}^2\,3\text{p}^4$, so one 3p orbital holds a spin pair and the repulsion between paired electrons makes one easier to remove. A is true but would *increase* the ionization energy; C is false (3p electrons are removed first); D is false (radius decreases across the period).

text:
The graph shows the first eight successive ionization energies of an element in period 3.

![Graph of log10(ionization energy) against number of electrons removed for 1 to 8 electrons, with a large jump between the 4th and 5th electrons](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.3_5.svg)

Which element is it?

A. Magnesium
B. Aluminium
C. Silicon
D. Phosphorus
ms: **C.** The large jump occurs between the 4th and 5th ionization energies, so four electrons are in the outer shell (the 5th is removed from the full second shell, closer to the nucleus). The element is in group 14: silicon. Mg (A) would show the jump after the 2nd, Al (B) after the 3rd and P (D) after the 5th electron.

text:
The lines in the ultraviolet region of the hydrogen emission spectrum (the Lyman series) become closer together as their frequency increases. A student calculated the difference in frequency, $\Delta\nu$, between each line and the next line of higher frequency, and plotted $\Delta\nu$ against the frequency of the line, $\nu$.

![Graph of frequency difference to next line against line frequency for the Lyman series; points from (2.47, 0.457) down to (3.20, 0.024) in units of 10^15 Hz, curve falling towards zero](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.3_6.svg)

(a) State what happens to the electron in a hydrogen atom at the convergence limit of the series. [1]

(b) Estimate, by extrapolating the graph, the frequency of the convergence limit. [1]

(c) Calculate the first ionization energy of hydrogen, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, using your answer to (b). Use sections 1 and 2 of the data booklet. [2]

(d) Explain why the lines in the series converge at higher frequency. [1]

(e) State the energy level to which the electron falls to produce the lines in this series. [1]
ms:
(a)
- electron is removed from the atom / the atom is ionized / electron moves to $n = \infty$ ✓

(b)
- $3.29 \times 10^{15}\ \text{Hz}$ ✓ (Accept answers in the range $3.25 \times 10^{15}$ to $3.32 \times 10^{15}\ \text{Hz}$.)

(c)
- $E = h\nu = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.29 \times 10^{15} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$ (per atom) ✓
- $2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \div 1000 = 1.31 \times 10^{3}\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Award ECF from (b). Award [1 max] for answer in $\text{J mol}^{-1}$ or for failing to multiply by $N_\text{A}$.

(d)
- energy levels get closer together as $n$ increases / converge at higher energy ✓

(e)
- $n = 1$ / the first (ground state) level ✓

text:
(a) Write the full electron configuration of a phosphorus atom. [1]

(b) Draw an orbital diagram (arrows in boxes) to represent the electrons in the 3s and 3p sublevels of a phosphorus atom. [2]

(c) State the number of unpaired electrons in a phosphorus atom. [1]

(d) Describe the shape of a p orbital. [1]

(e) State the total number of orbitals in the third main energy level ($n = 3$). [1]
ms:
(a)
- $1\text{s}^{2}\,2\text{s}^{2}\,2\text{p}^{6}\,3\text{s}^{2}\,3\text{p}^{3}$ ✓

Do not accept $[\text{Ne}]\,3\text{s}^2\,3\text{p}^3$ (full configuration required).

(b)
- 3s box contains two arrows of opposite spin ($\uparrow\downarrow$) ✓
- three separate 3p boxes each containing one arrow, all with parallel spins ($\uparrow\ \uparrow\ \uparrow$) ✓

Award [1 max] if electrons are paired in the 3p orbitals.

(c)
- $3$ ✓

(d)
- dumbbell shaped / two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus (along an axis) ✓

(e)
- $9$ ✓ (one 3s, three 3p, five 3d)

text:
(a) Write the condensed electron configurations of a chromium atom and a copper atom. [2]

(b) Write the condensed electron configurations of the $\ce{Cu+}$ and $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ions. [2]

(c) State the Pauli exclusion principle. [1]

(d) Deduce the number of unpaired electrons in a ground-state chromium atom. [1]

(e) Explain why the 4s sublevel is filled before the 3d sublevel in potassium and calcium atoms. [1]
ms:
(a)
- Cr: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{5}\,4\text{s}^{1}$ ✓
- Cu: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{10}\,4\text{s}^{1}$ ✓

Accept 4s written before 3d in either.

(b)
- $\ce{Cu+}$: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{10}$ ✓
- $\ce{Cu^2+}$: $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^{9}$ ✓

Award [1 max] if 4s electrons are retained (e.g. $[\text{Ar}]\,3\text{d}^9\,4\text{s}^1$ for $\ce{Cu+}$) but both ions otherwise correct.

(c)
- an orbital can hold a maximum of two electrons **and** they must have opposite spins ✓

(d)
- $6$ ✓ ECF from (a).

(e)
- 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d (for these atoms), and electrons occupy the lowest energy sublevel available first (Aufbau principle) ✓

text:
One line in the visible emission spectrum of hydrogen has a wavelength of $486\ \text{nm}$.

(a) Calculate the frequency of this radiation. Use section 2 of the data booklet. [1]

(b) Calculate the energy, in $\text{J}$, of one photon of this radiation. [1]

(c) This line is produced when an electron falls to the $n = 2$ level. The next line in this series, at lower frequency, has a wavelength of $656\ \text{nm}$ and is produced by the transition $n = 3 \rightarrow n = 2$. Deduce the transition responsible for the $486\ \text{nm}$ line. [1]

(d) Explain why the emission spectrum of hydrogen consists of lines rather than a continuous spectrum. [2]

(e) State how the energy of a photon changes as its wavelength decreases. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $\nu = \dfrac{c}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.00 \times 10^{8}}{486 \times 10^{-9}} = 6.17 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$/$\text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

(b)
- $E = h\nu = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 6.17 \times 10^{14} = 4.09 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$ ✓ ECF from (a).

(c)
- $n = 4 \rightarrow n = 2$ ✓ (the next line at higher frequency than $3 \rightarrow 2$)

(d)
- electrons can only occupy (discrete) energy levels / energy of the electron is quantized ✓
- transition between two levels emits a photon of a specific energy/frequency/wavelength, giving a line ✓

(e)
- energy increases ✓

text:
The graph shows the first ionization energies of the period 3 elements.

![First ionization energies of period 3 elements in kJ/mol: Na 496, Mg 738, Al 578, Si 787, P 1012, S 1000, Cl 1251, Ar 1521](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.3_10.svg)

(a) Explain the general increase in first ionization energy across period 3. [2]

(b) Explain why the first ionization energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium. [2]

(c) The second ionization energy of sodium is $4562\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Explain why it is much greater than the first ionization energy of sodium. [2]

(d) Predict how the first ionization energy of potassium compares with that of sodium. Explain your answer. [2]
ms:
(a)
- nuclear charge/number of protons increases ✓
- electrons are removed from the same main energy level/shell with similar shielding, so the attraction for the outer electron increases / atomic radius decreases ✓

(b)
- the electron removed from Al is in a 3p sublevel/orbital whereas that from Mg is in 3s ✓
- 3p is higher in energy/further from the nucleus/shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is less strongly attracted ✓

(c)
- second electron is removed from the second main energy level/2p, which is closer to the nucleus ✓
- experiences less shielding/greater effective nuclear charge (and is removed from a positive ion) ✓

(d)
- potassium has a lower first ionization energy (than $496\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) ✓
- outer electron (4s) is further from the nucleus/in a higher energy level **and** more shielded, outweighing the increase in nuclear charge ✓

How many atoms are present in $0.500\ \text{mol}$ of ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$?

$N_\text{A} = 6.02 \times 10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$

A. $3.01 \times 10^{23}$
B. $1.20 \times 10^{24}$
C. $6.02 \times 10^{23}$
D. $2.41 \times 10^{24}$
ms: **B.** Each $\ce{NH3}$ molecule has $4$ atoms: $0.500 \times 4 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.20 \times 10^{24}$. A is the number of molecules; C uses $1$ mol; D uses $1.00$ mol instead of $0.500$ mol.

The structure of butanedioic acid is shown.

![Displayed formula of butanedioic acid, HOOC-CH2-CH2-COOH, with all hydrogen atoms shown](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.4_2.svg)

What is the empirical formula of butanedioic acid?

A. $\ce{C4H6O4}$
B. $\ce{C2H3O2}$
C. $\ce{CHO}$
D. $\ce{C2H4O2}$
ms: **B.** The molecular formula is $\ce{C4H6O4}$ (A), and dividing by the highest common factor, $2$, gives $\ce{C2H3O2}$. C divides incorrectly; D miscounts the hydrogen atoms (it is the formula of ethanoic acid).

text:
$2.00\ \text{g}$ of sodium hydroxide, $\ce{NaOH}$, is dissolved in water and made up to $250.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of solution. What is the concentration of the solution? ($M_\text{r}(\ce{NaOH}) = 40.00$)

A. $0.00800\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
B. $0.0500\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
C. $0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
D. $8.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
ms: **C.** $n = 2.00/40.00 = 0.0500\ \text{mol}$; $c = 0.0500/0.2500 = 0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. A is $2.00/250$ (mass divided by volume in $\text{cm}^3$); B is the amount, not the concentration; D is $2.00/0.250$ (mass used instead of amount).

text:
Which sample contains the greatest number of **atoms**?

A. $2.0\ \text{g}$ of $\ce{H2}$
B. $4.0\ \text{g}$ of $\ce{He}$
C. $16\ \text{g}$ of $\ce{CH4}$
D. $32\ \text{g}$ of $\ce{O2}$
ms: **C.** Each sample is about $1$ mol of particles: A $\approx 1.0$ mol $\ce{H2}$ ($2$ mol atoms); B $1.0$ mol He ($1$ mol atoms); C $\approx 1.0$ mol $\ce{CH4}$ ($\approx 5$ mol atoms); D $1.0$ mol $\ce{O2}$ ($2$ mol atoms). Students counting molecules rather than atoms think all four are equal.

text:
$20\ \text{cm}^3$ of a gaseous hydrocarbon reacts completely with exactly $130\ \text{cm}^3$ of oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What is the formula of the hydrocarbon?

A. $\ce{C2H6}$
B. $\ce{C3H8}$
C. $\ce{C4H8}$
D. $\ce{C4H10}$
ms: **D.** By Avogadro's law the mole ratio hydrocarbon : $\ce{O2}$ is $20 : 130 = 1 : 6.5$. $\ce{C4H10 + 6.5O2 -> 4CO2 + 5H2O}$. The others need $3.5$ (A), $5$ (B) and $6$ (C) mol of $\ce{O2}$ per mol.

text:
A student determined the empirical formula of magnesium oxide by heating magnesium ribbon in a crucible, using the apparatus shown. The lid was lifted slightly from time to time during heating.

![Crucible with lid containing magnesium ribbon on a pipe-clay triangle on a tripod, heated by a Bunsen burner](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.4_6.svg)

| Measurement | Mass / g $\pm 0.001$ |
|---|---|
| empty crucible and lid | $25.402$ |
| crucible, lid and magnesium before heating | $25.645$ |
| crucible, lid and solid after heating to constant mass | $25.807$ |

(a) Calculate the mass of magnesium used and the mass of oxygen that combined with it. [1]

(b) Determine the empirical formula of magnesium oxide from these results. Use $A_\text{r}(\text{Mg}) = 24.31$ and $A_\text{r}(\text{O}) = 16.00$. [2]

(c) Suggest why the lid was lifted from time to time but not removed completely. [1]

(d) Some of the magnesium reacts with nitrogen in the air to form magnesium nitride, $\ce{Mg3N2}$. Explain the effect this would have on the experimental ratio of oxygen to magnesium. [2]
ms:
(a)
- Mg $= 0.243\ \text{g}$ **and** O $= 0.162\ \text{g}$ ✓

(b)
- $n(\text{Mg}) = \dfrac{0.243}{24.31} = 0.0100\ \text{mol}$ **and** $n(\text{O}) = \dfrac{0.162}{16.00} = 0.0101\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- ratio $1 : 1$ so $\ce{MgO}$ ✓

Award ECF from (a).

(c)
- lifting lets oxygen/air in for the magnesium to react **and** keeping the lid on prevents solid magnesium oxide (smoke) escaping ✓

(d)
- for each mole of Mg, less mass is gained when the nitride forms than when the oxide forms / the final mass is lower than if only $\ce{MgO}$ formed ✓
- so the calculated mass/amount of oxygen is too low and the O : Mg ratio is less than $1$ / lower than the true value ✓

text:
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate has the formula $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$.

(a) State the meaning of one mole of a substance. [1]

(b) Calculate the molar mass of $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$. Use section 7 of the data booklet. [1]

(c) Calculate the amount, in mol, of $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ in $5.00\ \text{g}$ of the solid. [1]

(d) Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in $5.00\ \text{g}$ of the solid. [2]

(e) Calculate the percentage by mass of water in $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- amount of substance containing $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ (the Avogadro constant number of) particles/elementary entities ✓

(b)
- $249.72\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ ✓ (Accept $249.7$ or $250$; $63.55 + 32.07 + 4(16.00) + 5(18.02)$.)

(c)
- $\dfrac{5.00}{249.72} = 0.0200\ \text{mol}$ ✓ ECF from (b).

(d)
- $9$ oxygen atoms per formula unit, so $9 \times 0.0200 = 0.180\ \text{mol}$ O ✓
- $0.180 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.08 \times 10^{23}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for $4$ or $5$ O per formula unit used ($4.82 \times 10^{22}$ or $6.02 \times 10^{22}$). ECF from (c).

(e)
- $\dfrac{90.10}{249.72} \times 100 = 36.1\ \%$ ✓

text:
A student prepares a standard solution of sodium carbonate, $\ce{Na2CO3}$.

(a) Calculate the mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate needed to make $250.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of a $0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ solution. [2]

(b) Outline how the student should prepare this standard solution from the solid. [3]

(c) $10.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of the standard solution is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of $100.0\ \text{cm}^3$. Calculate the concentration of the diluted solution in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. [1]

(d) Express the concentration of the diluted solution in $\text{g dm}^{-3}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $n = 0.100 \times 0.2500 = 0.0250\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $M_\text{r} = 105.99$; mass $= 0.0250 \times 105.99 = 2.65\ \text{g}$ ✓

(b)
- weigh the solid accurately (e.g. by difference on a balance) **and** dissolve it in a small volume of distilled water in a beaker ✓
- transfer the solution to a $250\ \text{cm}^3$ volumetric flask, rinsing the beaker (and funnel) into the flask ✓
- make up to the mark with distilled water (bottom of meniscus on the line) **and** stopper and invert to mix ✓

text:
(a) A $500\ \text{cm}^3$ sample of drinking water contains $0.250\ \text{mg}$ of dissolved lead(II) ions, $\ce{Pb^2+}$. The density of the water is $1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$.

(i) Calculate the concentration of lead(II) ions in parts per million (ppm) by mass. [2]

(ii) Calculate the concentration of lead(II) ions in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. [2]

(b) State Avogadro's law. [1]

(c) At the same temperature and pressure, $1.00\ \text{dm}^3$ of oxygen gas has a mass of $1.43\ \text{g}$ and $1.00\ \text{dm}^3$ of an unknown gas, Z, has a mass of $1.25\ \text{g}$. Determine the relative molecular mass of Z. [2]
ms:
(a)(i)
- mass of water $= 500\ \text{g}$ **and** mass of $\ce{Pb^2+} = 2.50 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{g}$ ✓
- $\dfrac{2.50 \times 10^{-4}}{500} \times 10^{6} = 0.500\ \text{ppm}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer.

(a)(ii)
- $n(\ce{Pb^2+}) = \dfrac{2.50 \times 10^{-4}}{207.2} = 1.21 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\dfrac{1.21 \times 10^{-6}}{0.500} = 2.41 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for $2.41 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ (mass in mg not converted to g).

(b)
- equal volumes of (all) gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain equal numbers of molecules/particles/moles ✓

(c)
- equal volumes contain equal amounts, so $\dfrac{M(\text{Z})}{M(\ce{O2})} = \dfrac{1.25}{1.43}$ ✓
- $M_\text{r} = 32.00 \times \dfrac{1.25}{1.43} = 28.0$ ✓

text:
Which is **not** an assumption of the ideal gas model?

A. The volume of the gas particles is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
B. There are no intermolecular forces between the particles.
C. Collisions between particles are perfectly elastic.
D. All the particles move at the same speed.
ms: **D.** In an ideal gas the particles have a range (distribution) of speeds; only the *average* kinetic energy is fixed by the temperature. A, B and C are all assumptions of the ideal gas model.

text:
Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?

A. High temperature and high pressure
B. High temperature and low pressure
C. Low temperature and high pressure
D. Low temperature and low pressure
ms: **B.** At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their volume is negligible; at high temperature they move fast, so intermolecular attractions are insignificant. High pressure (A, C) makes particle volume significant, and low temperature (C, D) makes attractions significant.

text:
What volume is occupied by $0.200\ \text{mol}$ of an ideal gas at $300\ \text{K}$ and $150\ \text{kPa}$?

$R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$

A. $3.32 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{dm}^3$
B. $3.32\ \text{dm}^3$
C. $33.2\ \text{dm}^3$
D. $3.32 \times 10^{3}\ \text{dm}^3$
ms: **B.** $V = \dfrac{nRT}{p} = \dfrac{0.200 \times 8.31 \times 300}{150 \times 10^{3}} = 3.32 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3 = 3.32\ \text{dm}^3$. A leaves the answer in $\text{m}^3$ but labels it $\text{dm}^3$; D uses $150\ \text{Pa}$ (and $\text{m}^3 \rightarrow \text{dm}^3$); C is a power-of-ten slip.

text:
A fixed mass of an ideal gas occupies $2.0\ \text{dm}^3$ at $27\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $100\ \text{kPa}$. The gas is heated to $327\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and its pressure changed to $200\ \text{kPa}$. What is the new volume?

A. $1.0\ \text{dm}^3$
B. $2.0\ \text{dm}^3$
C. $4.0\ \text{dm}^3$
D. $12\ \text{dm}^3$
ms: **B.** $V_2 = V_1 \times \dfrac{p_1}{p_2} \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.0 \times \dfrac{100}{200} \times \dfrac{600}{300} = 2.0\ \text{dm}^3$. D uses Celsius temperatures ($2.0 \times 0.5 \times 327/27 \approx 12$); A ignores the temperature change; C ignores the pressure change.

text:
Which graph shows the relationship for a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature?

![Four sketch graphs: A p against V, straight line through origin; B p against 1/V, straight line through origin; C pV against p, straight line with positive gradient and positive intercept; D p against V, straight line with negative gradient](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.5_5.svg)

A. A
B. B
C. C
D. D
ms: **B.** At constant temperature $pV = \text{constant}$, so $p \propto 1/V$: a plot of $p$ against $1/V$ is a straight line through the origin. A would mean $p \propto V$; C should be a horizontal line; D is the common error of drawing an inverse relationship as a straight line with negative gradient (the true $p$ against $V$ graph is a curve).

text:
A student determined the molar mass of the gas in a butane lighter by releasing gas under water and collecting it in an inverted measuring cylinder, as shown.

![Butane lighter under water releasing bubbles into an inverted measuring cylinder full of water, clamped in a trough](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.5_6.svg)

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| mass of lighter before | $25.648\ \text{g}$ |
| mass of lighter after (dried) | $25.518\ \text{g}$ |
| volume of gas collected | $56.0\ \text{cm}^3$ |
| temperature of water | $21.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$ |
| atmospheric pressure | $100.8\ \text{kPa}$ |

(a) Calculate the amount, in mol, of gas collected. Assume the gas behaves ideally and is at atmospheric pressure. [2]

(b) Calculate the molar mass of the gas. [1]

(c) The accepted molar mass of butane is $58.14\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the percentage error in the student's result. [1]

(d) The gas collected is saturated with water vapour. Explain how this affects the calculated molar mass. [2]

(e) Suggest **one** other possible source of error in this experiment. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $p = 100\,800\ \text{Pa}$, $V = 5.60 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{m}^3$, $T = 294.15\ \text{K}$ (all three conversions correct) ✓
- $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = \dfrac{100\,800 \times 5.60 \times 10^{-5}}{8.31 \times 294.15} = 2.31 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Accept $T = 294\ \text{K}$.

(b)
- mass $= 0.130\ \text{g}$; $M = \dfrac{0.130}{2.31 \times 10^{-3}} = 56.3\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ ✓ ECF from (a).

(c)
- $\dfrac{58.14 - 56.3}{58.14} \times 100 = 3.2\ \%$ ✓ ECF from (b). (Accept $3.1$ to $3.2\ \%$.)

(d)
- part of the volume/pressure of the collected gas is due to water vapour, so the amount of butane is overestimated ✓
- so the calculated molar mass is too low ✓

(e)
- lighter not completely dried before reweighing, so mass loss is too small / some butane dissolves in the water / gas escapes before entering the cylinder / pressure inside cylinder not equal to atmospheric (water levels inside and outside not equalized) / reading the volume (parallax) ✓

Accept any one valid error with a brief reason.

text:
The graph shows how $\dfrac{pV}{nRT}$ varies with pressure for nitrogen and carbon dioxide at the same constant temperature, above the critical temperature of both gases (illustrative data).

![Graph of pV/nRT against pressure from 0 to 60 MPa: ideal gas horizontal line at 1; N2 stays near 1 then rises to 1.4; CO2 falls to about 0.33 at 33 MPa then rises to 0.76 at 60 MPa](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.5_7.svg)

(a) State the value of $\dfrac{pV}{nRT}$ for an ideal gas at all pressures. [1]

(b) Explain why the value for carbon dioxide falls well below the ideal value as the pressure increases from $0$ to $30\ \text{MPa}$. [2]

(c) Explain why the value for nitrogen is greater than the ideal value at $60\ \text{MPa}$. [2]

(d) Predict, with a reason, how the curve for carbon dioxide would change if the measurements were repeated at a much higher temperature. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $1$ ✓

(b)
- (stronger) intermolecular forces/attractions between $\ce{CO2}$ molecules (which has more electrons than $\ce{N2}$) ✓
- at higher pressure molecules are closer together so the attractions reduce the pressure exerted on the walls/reduce the volume, so $pV < nRT$ ✓

(c)
- at high pressure the volume of the molecules themselves is no longer negligible compared with the container volume ✓
- so the actual volume of gas is greater than that predicted by the ideal gas model ($pV > nRT$) ✓

(d)
- curve closer to $1$/nearer the ideal line **because** molecules have more kinetic energy so intermolecular attractions are less significant ✓

text:
(a) State **two** assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas. [2]

(b) Calculate the volume, in $\text{dm}^3$, occupied by $3.20\ \text{g}$ of oxygen gas, $\ce{O2}$, at standard temperature and pressure (STP). Use section 2 of the data booklet. [2]

(c) A sealed, rigid container of gas is heated. Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of the gas increases. [2]
ms:
(a) Any two of:
- particles have negligible volume (compared with the container) ✓
- no intermolecular forces between particles ✓
- collisions are perfectly elastic ✓
- particles are in continuous random (straight-line) motion ✓
- average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature ✓

(b)
- $n(\ce{O2}) = \dfrac{3.20}{32.00} = 0.100\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $V = 0.100 \times 22.7 = 2.27\ \text{dm}^3$ ✓

Award [1 max] for $4.54\ \text{dm}^3$ (using $M = 16.00$). Accept $2.24\ \text{dm}^3$ if $22.4$ is used with the old STP definition.

(c)
- particles gain kinetic energy/move faster ✓
- so they collide with the walls more frequently **and** with greater force ✓

text:
A gaseous hydrocarbon, G, contains $85.6\ \%$ carbon and $14.4\ \%$ hydrogen by mass.

(a) Determine the empirical formula of G. [2]

(b) $0.535\ \text{g}$ of G occupies $250.0\ \text{cm}^3$ at $50.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $101.3\ \text{kPa}$. Calculate the molar mass of G. [3]

(c) Deduce the molecular formula of G. [1]

(d) The true molar mass of G is slightly lower than the value obtained in (b). Suggest a reason, related to the ideal gas model, for this difference. [1]
ms:
(a)
- C: $\dfrac{85.6}{12.01} = 7.13$; H: $\dfrac{14.4}{1.01} = 14.3$ ✓
- ratio $1 : 2$ so $\ce{CH2}$ ✓

(b)
- conversions: $V = 2.500 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3$ **and** $T = 323.15\ \text{K}$ **and** $p = 101\,300\ \text{Pa}$ ✓
- $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = \dfrac{101\,300 \times 2.500 \times 10^{-4}}{8.31 \times 323.15} = 9.43 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $M = \dfrac{0.535}{9.43 \times 10^{-3}} = 56.7\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [3] for correct final answer. Accept $56.7$ to $56.8$. Accept kPa with $\text{dm}^3$ ($V = 0.2500\ \text{dm}^3$) for M1.

(c)
- $\dfrac{56.7}{14.03} \approx 4$, so $\ce{C4H8}$ ✓ ECF from (a) and (b).

(d)
- intermolecular attractions between molecules of G make the real volume (or pressure) smaller than ideal, so the calculated amount is too small and $M$ too large ✓

Accept "G is not an ideal gas / G deviates from ideal behaviour because of intermolecular forces" with some explanation.

text:
A rigid $5.00\ \text{dm}^3$ steel cylinder contains helium at $20.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and $250\ \text{kPa}$.

(a) Calculate the amount, in mol, of helium in the cylinder. [2]

(b) The cylinder is heated to $80.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Calculate the new pressure inside the cylinder. [2]

(c) At $20.0\ ^\circ\text{C}$, all of the helium is transferred into a balloon, where its pressure is $100\ \text{kPa}$. Calculate the volume of the balloon. [1]

(d) Sketch a graph to show how the pressure of the helium in the cylinder varies with its kelvin temperature. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $n = \dfrac{pV}{RT} = \dfrac{250 \times 10^{3} \times 5.00 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 293.15}$ ✓
- $0.513\ \text{mol}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Award [1 max] for use of $T = 20.0$.

(b)
- $p_2 = p_1 \times \dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 250 \times \dfrac{353.15}{293.15}$ ✓
- $301\ \text{kPa}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for $1000\ \text{kPa}$ (Celsius temperatures used).

(c)
- $V_2 = \dfrac{250 \times 5.00}{100} = 12.5\ \text{dm}^3$ ✓

(d)
- axes labelled pressure and temperature/K ✓
- straight line with positive gradient that passes through (or extrapolates to) the origin ✓

![Expected sketch: straight line through the origin for pressure against kelvin temperature](qbank/img/gen_chem_S1.5_10-2.svg)

text:
Which name and formula are correctly matched?

A. calcium hydrogencarbonate, $\ce{CaHCO3}$
B. ammonium phosphate, $\ce{(NH4)3PO4}$
C. aluminium sulfate, $\ce{Al3(SO4)2}$
D. sodium nitrate, $\ce{NaNO2}$
ms: **B.** $\ce{NH4+}$ and $\ce{PO4^3-}$ combine 3 : 1 so the charges cancel. A should be $\ce{Ca(HCO3)2}$ (two 1− ions balance $\ce{Ca^2+}$); C swaps the subscripts, it should be $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$; D is sodium nitrite – nitrate is $\ce{NO3-}$, giving $\ce{NaNO3}$.

text:
Which ion has the same electron configuration as an argon atom?

A. $\ce{Na+}$
B. $\ce{Mg^2+}$
C. $\ce{Ca^2+}$
D. $\ce{F-}$
ms: **C.** Ca ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2$) loses its two 4s electrons to give $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6$, the configuration of Ar. $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{F-}$ are all isoelectronic with neon, not argon.

text:
Which compound is expected to have the largest lattice enthalpy?

A. $\ce{NaF}$
B. $\ce{KBr}$
C. $\ce{MgO}$
D. $\ce{CaO}$
ms: **C.** Lattice enthalpy increases with greater ionic charge and smaller ionic radius. MgO and CaO both have 2+/2− ions (stronger attraction than the 1+/1− ions in NaF and KBr); $\ce{Mg^2+}$ is smaller than $\ce{Ca^2+}$, so MgO has the larger value. NaF is the trap for students who only consider ion size.

text:
Which properties are typical of ionic compounds?

I. high melting point
II. conduct electricity when molten
III. conduct electricity when solid

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** Strong electrostatic attraction in the giant lattice gives high melting points (I), and molten ionic compounds have mobile ions that carry charge (II). In the solid the ions are fixed in the lattice and there are no delocalized electrons, so III is false.

text:
The diagram shows part of the lattice of sodium chloride.

![part of the sodium chloride lattice showing alternating sodium and chloride ions in a cubic arrangement](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.1_5.svg)

How many oppositely charged ions surround each ion as nearest neighbours?

A. 4
B. 6
C. 8
D. 12
ms: **B.** In the NaCl lattice each $\ce{Na+}$ is surrounded octahedrally by six $\ce{Cl-}$ ions (above, below, left, right, front, back) and each $\ce{Cl-}$ by six $\ce{Na+}$ ions (6 : 6 coordination). 8 is the coordination number in CsCl; 12 is counting same-charge next-nearest neighbours; 4 is what is seen in a single 2-D layer.

text:
A student investigates the sodium halides. The graph shows their melting points plotted against the sum of the ionic radii of the cation and anion.

![graph of melting point against sum of ionic radii for NaF, NaCl, NaBr and NaI; melting point decreases as the sum of radii increases](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.1_6.svg)

(a) Describe the relationship shown by the graph. [1]

(b) Explain the relationship in terms of the bonding in the sodium halides. [2]

(c) Magnesium oxide, $\ce{MgO}$, has a sum of ionic radii (212 pm) only slightly smaller than that of sodium fluoride but a melting point of 2852 °C. Explain this difference. [2]

(d) The student tests the electrical conductivity of solid sodium chloride and of molten sodium chloride. Predict the results and explain them. [2]
ms:
(a)
- melting point decreases as the sum of the ionic radii increases ✓ *Accept "inverse/negative correlation".*

(b)
- larger ions so greater distance between the centres of the ions / lower charge density ✓
- weaker electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions so less energy needed to break up the lattice ✓

(c)
- $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{O^2-}$ have double the charge of $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{F-}$ ✓
- (much) stronger electrostatic attraction between ions / larger lattice enthalpy ✓

(d)
- solid does not conduct AND molten does conduct ✓
- ions fixed in position in the solid lattice but mobile/free to move in the molten state ✓ *Do not accept "electrons move" for molten NaCl.*

text:
Magnesium reacts with nitrogen when it is burned in air, forming the ionic compound magnesium nitride.

(a) State the full electron configurations of the magnesium ion and the nitride ion. [2]

(b) Deduce the formula of magnesium nitride. [1]

(c) Describe the bonding in magnesium nitride. [2]

(d) Explain why the magnesium ion is smaller than the sodium ion. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $\ce{Mg^2+}$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ ✓
- $\ce{N^3-}$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$ ✓

(b)
- $\ce{Mg3N2}$ ✓

(c)
- electrons are transferred from Mg atoms to N atoms forming $\ce{Mg^2+}$ and $\ce{N^3-}$ ions ✓
- (lattice held by) electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions ✓

(d)
- both ions have the same electron configuration/number of electrons/are isoelectronic ✓
- Mg has one more proton/greater nuclear charge, so electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus ✓

text:
Lattice enthalpy values for some ionic compounds are given.

| compound | lattice enthalpy / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| $\ce{LiF}$ | 1049 |
| $\ce{NaCl}$ | 790 |
| $\ce{KBr}$ | 691 |
| $\ce{CaO}$ | 3401 |
| $\ce{MgO}$ | 3791 |

(a) Define the term *lattice enthalpy*. [2]

(b) Explain why the lattice enthalpy of $\ce{MgO}$ is much greater than that of $\ce{NaCl}$. [2]

(c) Explain why the lattice enthalpy of $\ce{MgO}$ is greater than that of $\ce{CaO}$. [2]

(d) Ionic solids such as magnesium oxide are brittle. Explain this property in terms of the structure of the lattice. [2]
ms:
(a)
- enthalpy change when one mole of a solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions ✓
- under standard conditions / (it is) endothermic ✓ *Accept the reverse process (formation of lattice from gaseous ions) if the sign is given as negative/exothermic.*

(b)
- $\ce{Mg^2+}$ / $\ce{O^2-}$ have greater charges than $\ce{Na+}$ / $\ce{Cl-}$ ✓
- (and are smaller) so stronger electrostatic attraction between ions ✓

(c)
- $\ce{Mg^2+}$ is smaller than $\ce{Ca^2+}$ / same charge but smaller radius / greater charge density ✓
- shorter distance between ion centres so stronger attraction ✓

(d)
- a force displaces layers of ions so that ions of the same charge become next to each other ✓
- repulsion between like charges causes the lattice to split/shatter ✓

text:
A Group 2 element, X, forms an ionic chloride with formula $\ce{XCl2}$. Analysis shows that 1.000 g of $\ce{XCl2}$ contains 0.6389 g of chlorine.

(a) Determine the relative atomic mass of X and identify the element. [3]

(b) Explain why $\ce{XCl2}$ conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not as a solid. [2]

(c) Use the electronegativity values Ca 1.0, Al 1.6 and Cl 3.2 to compare the electronegativity differences in $\ce{XCl2}$ and aluminium chloride, $\ce{AlCl3}$. [1]

(d) Aluminium chloride sublimes at 180 °C whereas $\ce{XCl2}$ melts at 772 °C. Suggest, with reference to your answer to (c), why the two chlorides differ so much. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $n(\ce{Cl}) = \frac{0.6389}{35.45} = 0.01802\ \text{mol}$ AND $n(\ce{X}) = 0.009011\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $m(\ce{X}) = 1.000 - 0.6389 = 0.3611\ \text{g}$, so $A_r = \frac{0.3611}{0.009011} = 40.1$ ✓
- calcium/Ca ✓
*Award [3] for correct final answer with working. Accept 40.0–40.2.*

(b)
- in aqueous solution ions are free to move/mobile ✓
- in the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice ✓

(c)
- $\Delta\chi$: $\ce{CaCl2}$ = 2.2 AND $\ce{AlCl3}$ = 1.6 ✓ *ECF from (a) for the identity of X.*

(d)
- $\ce{CaCl2}$ has (predominantly) ionic bonding/giant ionic lattice with strong attraction between ions ✓
- $\ce{AlCl3}$ has significant covalent character/is polar covalent, existing as (small) molecules with weak intermolecular forces ✓
*Accept answers referring to the high charge density of $\ce{Al^3+}$ polarizing the chloride ion.*

text:
What is the molecular geometry and the approximate H–N–H bond angle in ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$?

A. trigonal planar, 120°
B. trigonal pyramidal, 107°
C. tetrahedral, 109.5°
D. trigonal pyramidal, 104.5°
ms: **B.** N has four electron domains (three bonding pairs and one lone pair): the electron domain geometry is tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry is trigonal pyramidal. The lone pair repels more strongly than the bonding pairs, reducing the angle from 109.5° to about 107°. C confuses the electron domain and molecular geometry; 104.5° is the angle for water (two lone pairs).

text:
Which molecule is polar?

A. $\ce{CO2}$
B. $\ce{CCl4}$
C. $\ce{CH2Cl2}$
D. $\ce{BF3}$
ms: **C.** $\ce{CH2Cl2}$ is tetrahedral but the C–Cl and C–H bond dipoles are different, so they do not cancel and there is a net dipole moment. A, B and D all contain polar bonds, but their symmetrical shapes (linear, tetrahedral with identical substituents, trigonal planar) cancel the bond dipoles.

text:
Which compound has the highest boiling point?

A. $\ce{CH3CH2CH3}$
B. $\ce{CH3OCH3}$
C. $\ce{CH3CH2OH}$
D. $\ce{CH3CHO}$
ms: **C.** The four compounds have similar molar masses (44–46 $\text{g mol}^{-1}$), so London dispersion forces are similar. Only ethanol has an O–H bond and can form hydrogen bonds between molecules. Methoxymethane and ethanal are polar (dipole–dipole forces) but cannot hydrogen bond with each other; propane has only dispersion forces.

text:
Which species contain a coordination (dative) covalent bond?

I. $\ce{NH4+}$
II. $\ce{H3O+}$
III. $\ce{NH3}$

A. I only
B. I and II only
C. I and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **B.** In $\ce{NH4+}$ the lone pair on N, and in $\ce{H3O+}$ a lone pair on O, is donated to an $\ce{H+}$ ion that has no electrons, forming a coordination bond. In $\ce{NH3}$ each N–H bond is formed from one electron from each atom; the lone pair is not used in bonding.

text:
A Lewis formula for the sulfate ion, $\ce{SO4^2-}$, is drawn with four S–O single bonds and no lone pairs on the sulfur atom. What is the formal charge on the sulfur atom in this structure?

A. −2
B. 0
C. +2
D. +6
ms: **C.** FC = (valence electrons) − ½(bonding electrons) − (non-bonding electrons) = 6 − ½(8) − 0 = +2. Zero is the formal charge in the alternative structure with two S=O double bonds (the preferred structure); +6 is the oxidation state of S, not its formal charge; −2 is the charge of the whole ion.

text:
The structure of propenenitrile is shown.

![skeletal structure of propenenitrile, CH2=CH–C≡N](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.2_6.svg)

How many sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds are present in one molecule of propenenitrile, $\ce{CH2=CHCN}$?

A. 6 σ and 3 π
B. 6 σ and 2 π
C. 7 σ and 3 π
D. 9 σ and 0 π
ms: **A.** Three C–H bonds (3 σ), C=C (1 σ + 1 π), C–C (1 σ) and C≡N (1 σ + 2 π): 6 σ and 3 π. B treats the triple bond as having only one π bond; C counts one σ bond too many (e.g. counting the C≡N as two σ bonds); D counts every line in the structure as a σ bond.

text:
A student uses paper chromatography to analyse a food colouring, X, and compares it with three reference dyes, R1, R2 and R3. The chromatogram obtained is shown.

![paper chromatogram: lane X has spots at 2.4, 4.0 and 6.8 cm; R1 at 2.4 cm; R2 at 5.2 cm; R3 at 6.8 cm; solvent front at 8.0 cm above the baseline](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.2_7.svg)

(a) Calculate the $R_F$ value of the spot in X that travelled 4.0 cm. [1]

(b) Deduce which reference dye(s) are present in X. [1]

(c) Explain why the baseline is drawn in pencil and must be above the level of the solvent at the start. [2]

(d) R3 travels further than R1. Explain this observation in terms of the stationary and mobile phases. [2]
ms:
(a)
- $R_F = \frac{4.0}{8.0} = 0.50$ ✓ *Accept 0.5.*

(b)
- R1 and R3 (but not R2) ✓

(c)
- pencil (graphite) is insoluble in the solvent / ink would dissolve and separate/run ✓
- if below solvent level the dyes would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker/container instead of moving up the paper ✓

(d)
- R3 is more soluble in/has a greater affinity for the mobile phase (solvent) ✓
- R1 is more strongly attracted to/adsorbed by the stationary phase (water in the paper / cellulose) ✓
*Accept answers in terms of relative polarity of the dyes and phases.*

text:
The graph shows the boiling points of the hydrides of the elements in groups 14 to 17 for periods 2 to 5.

![graph of boiling point against period for group 14, 15, 16 and 17 hydrides; NH3, H2O and HF are anomalously high in period 2](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.2_8.svg)

(a) Explain the increase in boiling point from $\ce{CH4}$ to $\ce{SnH4}$. [2]

(b) Explain why the boiling points of $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{HF}$ do not follow the trend shown by the other hydrides in their groups. [2]

(c) The H–F bond is more polar than the H–O bond, yet water has the higher boiling point. Suggest why. [2]

(d) State why the group 14 hydrides have the lowest boiling point in each period. [1]
ms:
(a)
- number of electrons/molar mass/size of electron cloud increases ✓
- (so) stronger London (dispersion) forces between molecules ✓

(b)
- N, O and F are highly electronegative/small and bonded directly to H so the molecules form hydrogen bonds ✓
- hydrogen bonds are stronger than the dipole–dipole/London forces between the other hydrides, so more energy is needed to separate molecules ✓

(c)
- each water molecule has two H atoms and two lone pairs so can form (on average) two hydrogen bonds per molecule ✓
- HF has one H atom per molecule, so (on average) only one hydrogen bond per molecule / fewer hydrogen bonds in total ✓

(d)
- (tetrahedral and) non-polar so only London (dispersion) forces between molecules ✓

text:
The table shows data for three compounds of similar molar mass.

| compound | formula | $M$ / $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ | boiling point / °C |
|---|---|---|---|
| butane | $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH3}$ | 58.14 | −0.5 |
| propanone | $\ce{CH3COCH3}$ | 58.09 | 56 |
| propan-1-ol | $\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}$ | 60.11 | 97 |

(a) Explain the order of boiling points in terms of the intermolecular forces present. [4]

(b) Predict, with a reason, which of butane and propan-1-ol is more soluble in water. [2]

(c) Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide are covalent network structures.

(i) Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. [2]

(ii) Explain why silicon dioxide has a much higher melting point than carbon dioxide. [2]
ms:
(a)
- all three have London (dispersion) forces of similar strength (similar molar mass/number of electrons) ✓
- butane is non-polar/has only London forces so lowest boiling point ✓
- propanone is polar/has (permanent) dipole–dipole forces in addition ✓
- propan-1-ol forms hydrogen bonds (O–H group), the strongest intermolecular force, so highest boiling point ✓

(b)
- propan-1-ol ✓
- can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (butane cannot) ✓

(c)(i)
- in graphite each C is bonded to three others leaving one delocalized electron per atom (between the layers) ✓
- in diamond all four valence electrons are used in (localized) covalent bonds, so no mobile electrons ✓

(c)(ii)
- $\ce{SiO2}$ is a covalent network/giant covalent structure: melting requires breaking strong covalent bonds ✓
- $\ce{CO2}$ is a simple molecular substance: only weak intermolecular (London) forces are overcome ✓

text:
Boron trifluoride, $\ce{BF3}$, reacts with ammonia, $\ce{NH3}$, to form a single product, $\ce{F3B-NH3}$.

(a) Draw the Lewis formulas of $\ce{BF3}$ and $\ce{NH3}$. [2]

(b) State the molecular geometry and bond angle of $\ce{BF3}$ and of $\ce{NH3}$. [2]

(c) Describe how the bond between nitrogen and boron forms in $\ce{F3B-NH3}$. [2]

(d) Predict the F–B–F bond angle in $\ce{F3B-NH3}$ and explain your answer. [2]

(e) Explain why $\ce{BF3}$ is a non-polar molecule although the B–F bonds are polar. [1]
ms:
(a)
- $\ce{BF3}$: B with three single bonds to F, no lone pair on B, three lone pairs on each F ✓
- $\ce{NH3}$: N with three single bonds to H and one lone pair ✓

(b)
- $\ce{BF3}$: trigonal planar, 120° ✓
- $\ce{NH3}$: trigonal pyramidal, 107° ✓ *Accept 106–108°.*

(c)
- coordination/dative covalent bond ✓
- the lone pair on N is donated into the empty orbital of B / B has an incomplete octet and accepts the electron pair ✓

(d)
- 109.5° / approximately 109° ✓ *Accept "slightly less than 109.5°".*
- B now has four electron domains, all bonding pairs, so the arrangement around B is tetrahedral ✓

(e)
- symmetrical (trigonal planar) shape so the three bond dipoles cancel / no net dipole moment ✓

text:
The nitrate ion, $\ce{NO3-}$, can be represented by several Lewis formulas.

(a) Draw the Lewis formulas of the resonance structures of the nitrate ion. [2]

(b) Determine the formal charge on the nitrogen atom and on each oxygen atom in one of your structures. [2]

(c) The nitrogen–oxygen bonds in the nitrate ion are all the same length. Predict how this length compares with the N–O single bond and N=O double bond lengths, and explain your prediction. [2]

(d) State the hybridization of the nitrogen atom and the O–N–O bond angle. [2]

(e) Describe, in terms of the overlap of orbitals, how a delocalized π system forms in the nitrate ion. [2]
ms:
(a)
- one correct Lewis formula with one N=O and two N–O bonds, all lone pairs on O, and the overall charge shown (square brackets with −) ✓
- three equivalent structures drawn with the double bond in different positions / double-headed arrows between them ✓

(b)
- N: +1 ✓
- doubly bonded O: 0 AND each singly bonded O: −1 ✓

(c)
- between the single and double bond lengths ✓
- electrons delocalized over all three bonds / each bond has a bond order of $\frac{4}{3}$ / resonance hybrid ✓

(d)
- $sp^2$ ✓
- 120° ✓

(e)
- each atom has an unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the ion ✓
- the p orbitals overlap sideways (above and below the plane) so the π electrons are spread over all four atoms ✓

text:
Sulfur tetrafluoride, $\ce{SF4}$, and xenon tetrafluoride, $\ce{XeF4}$, both contain four bonds to fluorine.

(a) Deduce the Lewis formula of $\ce{SF4}$. [1]

(b) For each molecule, deduce the electron domain geometry and the molecular geometry. [4]

(c) Predict, with a reason, whether each molecule is polar. [2]

(d) Calculate the formal charge on the sulfur atom in $\ce{SF4}$. [1]
ms:
(a)
- S with four single bonds to F, one lone pair on S, three lone pairs on each F ✓ *Accept lines, dots or crosses for electron pairs.*

(b)
- $\ce{SF4}$: five electron domains, electron domain geometry trigonal bipyramidal ✓
- $\ce{SF4}$ molecular geometry: see-saw ✓
- $\ce{XeF4}$: six electron domains, electron domain geometry octahedral ✓
- $\ce{XeF4}$ molecular geometry: square planar ✓

(c)
- $\ce{SF4}$ polar AND $\ce{XeF4}$ non-polar ✓
- see-saw shape is asymmetric so bond dipoles do not cancel, whereas in square planar $\ce{XeF4}$ the bond dipoles cancel ✓

(d)
- FC = 6 − 2 − ½(8) = 0 ✓

text:
Which description of metallic bonding is correct?

A. electrostatic attraction between positive ions and negative ions
B. electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalized electrons
C. sharing of a pair of electrons between two metal atoms
D. electrostatic attraction between metal atoms and delocalized protons
ms: **B.** Metallic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and a "sea" of delocalized valence electrons. A describes ionic bonding and C covalent bonding; D is nonsense (protons are not delocalized).

text:
Which of these metals has the highest melting point?

A. sodium
B. magnesium
C. aluminium
D. potassium
ms: **C.** Aluminium forms $\ce{Al^3+}$ ions and contributes three delocalized electrons per atom; the ions are small, so the metallic bonding is strongest (m.p. 660 °C, compared with Mg 650 °C, Na 98 °C, K 63 °C). Students who think only of position in the group may pick B.

text:
Which statement explains why metals are malleable?

A. The delocalized electrons can move through the lattice when a voltage is applied.
B. The metal ions are held in fixed positions by strong covalent bonds.
C. Layers of cations can slide over each other while the delocalized electrons keep holding them together.
D. When a force is applied, ions of the same charge are brought next to each other.
ms: **C.** Metallic bonding is non-directional: when layers of cations slide, the delocalized electrons still attract them, so the metal changes shape without breaking. A explains conductivity, not malleability; B is wrong (no covalent bonds); D explains the brittleness of ionic solids.

text:
Iron melts at 1538 °C whereas calcium, also in period 4, melts at 842 °C. Which statement best explains this difference?

A. Iron has a larger atomic radius than calcium.
B. Both 3d and 4s electrons are delocalized in iron, giving stronger metallic bonding.
C. Iron forms ions with a 3+ charge only.
D. Iron atoms are held together by covalent bonds between d orbitals.
ms: **B.** In transition elements the 3d and 4s sublevels are close in energy, so d electrons as well as s electrons are delocalized. More delocalized electrons and smaller cations give stronger electrostatic attraction. A is false (Fe is smaller); C is false (Fe forms 2+ and 3+); D is not the model used for metals.

text:
The graph shows the melting points of the Group 1 metals plotted against the ionic radius of their $\ce{M+}$ ions.

![graph of melting point against ionic radius of M+ for Li, Na, K, Rb and Cs; melting point decreases from 180 °C for Li to 28 °C for Cs](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.3_5.svg)

(a) Describe the trend shown by the graph. [1]

(b) Explain the trend in terms of metallic bonding. [2]

(c) Explain why sodium conducts electricity both as a solid and as a liquid. [1]

(d) A student plans to compare the electrical conductivities of copper and aluminium by measuring the current through a wire of each metal connected to a battery.

(i) State the independent variable in this investigation. [1]

(ii) State **two** variables that must be controlled. [2]
ms:
(a)
- melting point decreases as the ionic radius increases/down the group ✓

(b)
- (all ions are 1+ but) larger ions mean the delocalized electrons are further from the nucleus/cation centre ✓
- weaker electrostatic attraction between the cations and delocalized electrons so less energy needed to melt ✓

(c)
- delocalized electrons are free to move in both solid and liquid ✓

(d)(i)
- the metal (copper or aluminium) / identity of the metal ✓

(d)(ii)
Any two:
- length of wire ✓
- cross-sectional area/diameter/gauge of wire ✓
- voltage/potential difference of the supply ✓
- temperature of the wire ✓

text:
(a) Describe the structure and bonding in solid magnesium. [2]

(b) Explain why magnesium is a good conductor of heat. [1]

(c) Magnesium melts at 650 °C and sodium melts at 98 °C. Explain this difference. [3]

(d) Suggest why the melting point of a metal is often a poorer guide to the strength of its metallic bonding than its boiling point. [1]
ms:
(a)
- lattice of $\ce{Mg^2+}$ ions/cations ✓
- (surrounded by) delocalized electrons, with electrostatic attraction between the cations and delocalized electrons ✓

(b)
- delocalized electrons (and vibrating ions) transfer kinetic energy through the lattice ✓

(c)
- Mg forms 2+ ions whereas Na forms 1+ ions ✓
- Mg contributes two delocalized electrons per atom compared with one for Na / Mg ion is smaller ✓
- stronger electrostatic attraction between cations and delocalized electrons in Mg ✓

(d)
- on melting the metallic bonding is not broken/the ions and electrons remain attracted (only the regular arrangement is lost); on boiling the atoms are completely separated ✓

text:
Copper and zinc are neighbouring elements in period 4.

(a) State the full electron configuration of a copper atom and of a $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ion. [2]

(b) Explain why transition metals such as copper generally have higher melting points and higher densities than calcium. [2]

(c) Copper melts at 1085 °C but zinc melts at only 420 °C. Suggest a reason for this difference in terms of the electrons available for metallic bonding. [2]

(d) Copper is used for electrical wiring. Explain why the electrical conductivity of copper decreases as its temperature rises. [1]
ms:
(a)
- Cu: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10} 4s^1$ ✓ *Accept $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1$; do not accept $3d^9 4s^2$.*
- $\ce{Cu^2+}$: $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^9$ ✓

(b)
- 3d as well as 4s electrons are delocalized / more delocalized electrons per atom, giving stronger metallic bonding (higher m.p.) ✓
- smaller atomic radius/increased nuclear charge with greater mass, so atoms are packed more closely and more massive (higher density) ✓

(c)
- Zn has a full/stable $3d^{10}$ sublevel with two 4s electrons ✓
- its d electrons are held more tightly/are less available for delocalization, so fewer delocalized electrons and weaker metallic bonding ✓

(d)
- cations vibrate more, so the delocalized electrons collide with them more often (greater resistance) ✓

text:
Four substances, W, X, Y and Z, are plotted on the bonding triangle.

![bonding triangle with points W near the metallic vertex, X near the covalent vertex, Y near the ionic vertex and Z in the polar covalent region](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.4_1.svg)

Which substance is most likely to be malleable and to conduct electricity in the solid state?

A. W
B. X
C. Y
D. Z
ms: **A.** W has a low average electronegativity and a small electronegativity difference, so it lies near the metallic vertex: metallic bonding gives malleability and conduction by delocalized electrons. Y is ionic (conducts only when molten or aqueous), X is covalent and Z is polar covalent; none have delocalized electrons in the solid.

text:
Why are alloys usually harder than the pure metals from which they are made?

A. The added element forms ionic bonds with the metal atoms.
B. Atoms of different sizes disrupt the regular layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other easily.
C. Alloys contain more delocalized electrons per atom than pure metals.
D. The added atoms fill all the spaces between metal ions, preventing the electrons from moving.
ms: **B.** Atoms of a different size distort the regular lattice, making it harder for layers to slide, so the alloy is harder/less malleable. Alloys are still metallic (not ionic, A); C is not the general reason; D is wrong because alloys still conduct electricity.

text:
A section of an addition polymer is shown.

![displayed formula of a polymer chain of six carbon atoms, each carbon bonded to one H and one CH3 group](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.4_3.svg)

Which monomer was used to make this polymer?

A. propene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH3}$
B. but-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CHCH2CH3}$
C. but-2-ene, $\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3}$
D. 2-methylpropene, $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)2}$
ms: **C.** The repeating unit is $\ce{-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-}$: both carbons of the original C=C carry one H and one $\ce{CH3}$, which is but-2-ene. Propene would give a $\ce{CH3}$ group only on alternate backbone carbons; but-1-ene gives ethyl side groups on alternate carbons; 2-methylpropene gives two $\ce{CH3}$ groups on alternate carbons.

text:
Which pairs of monomers can react to form a condensation polymer?

I. hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid
II. ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid
III. ethene and chloroethene

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** Each monomer in I and II has two functional groups that react, eliminating water: I gives a polyamide (nylon-6,6), II gives a polyester (PET). Ethene and chloroethene in III have C=C bonds and form an addition copolymer with no small molecule lost.

text:
A student investigates the effect of adding nickel to copper on the hardness of the alloy. The results are shown (illustrative data).

![graph of Vickers hardness against percentage of nickel: 50 HV at 0 %, 75 at 10 %, 95 at 20 %, 110 at 30 %, 120 at 40 %, 125 at 50 %](qbank/img/gen_chem_S2.4_5.svg)

(a) Describe the effect of the percentage of nickel on the hardness of the alloy. [2]

(b) Estimate, using the graph, the hardness of an alloy containing 25 % nickel by mass. [1]

(c) Explain, in terms of structure, why adding nickel increases the hardness of copper. [2]

(d) State the dependent variable and one variable that should be kept constant in this investigation. [2]
ms:
(a)
- hardness increases as the percentage of nickel increases ✓
- the rate of increase decreases / the curve levels off at higher percentages ✓

(b)
- 103 HV ✓ *Accept 100–106 HV.*

(c)
- nickel atoms have a different size from copper atoms and distort/disrupt the regular lattice ✓
- layers of atoms cannot slide over each other as easily ✓

(d)
- dependent: hardness (Vickers number) ✓
